00254.mechanism: Nonsteroidal, reversible aromatase inhibitor; reduces peripheral conversion of androgens to oestrogens. It is not an ovarian-suppression drug or an ER degrader.

00254.duration: NCCP consultant-directed duration according to setting, benefit and tolerance. Distinguish initial adjuvant, switch after 2–3 years tamoxifen, and advanced treatment. Do not universalise indefinite treatment or a five-year reset.

No mild/moderate hepatic reduction; linked SmPC cautions moderate/severe hepatic dysfunction. NCCP severe hepatic disease not recommended: withhold pending review rather than invent a reduction.
00254.source_scope: NCCP includes adjuvant and switch indications; linked Anastrozole Teva SmPC has narrower advanced indication wording. NCCP eligibility also mentions tamoxifen contraindication/intolerance.

00371.mechanism: Nonsteroidal, reversible aromatase inhibitor; oestrogen deprivation rather than ER antagonism or ovarian suppression.
00371.administration: 2.5 mg PO daily, continuous, with/without food; missed dose take when remembered unless next due within about 2–3 h, then skip; no doubling.
00371.duration: NCCP neoadjuvant 4–8 months to allow tumour reduction with response/surgery review; inadequate response prompts surgery and/or other options. Adjuvant, extended and advanced duration are separate.
00371.organ_function: NCCP no renal adjustment including haemodialysis expected; HPRA CrCl <10 lacks sufficient data and requires careful benefit/risk review. Child–Pugh A/B no adjustment. C: NCCP 50% original average dose = 2.5 mg every other day; HPRA close supervision without this numerical instruction. Reconcile current reduced/custom schedule first.
00371.source_scope: NCCP 00371d broad HR-positive neoadjuvant wording; SmPC additionally HER2-negative, chemotherapy unsuitable and immediate surgery not indicated. Separate optional fields flag known conflicts; missing values remain unassessed.

00376.mechanism: Steroidal, irreversible aromatase inactivator. It mimics an androgen substrate and inactivates the enzyme; it does not degrade the oestrogen receptor. This mechanism does not establish superiority or interchangeable sequencing with nonsteroidal AIs.
00376.administration: 25 mg PO once daily, continuous, preferably after a meal; swallow whole without chewing/crushing; skip missed dose.
00376.duration: NCCP broad adjuvant/extended/advanced pathways. Aromasin label specifically 2–3 years tamoxifen then exemestane to total 5 years; extension is separate. Advanced continuation follows benefit/tolerance.
00376.organ_function: NCCP no renal/hepatic dose adjustment, haemodialysis expected no adjustment; linked SmPC caution. Strong CYP3A4 inducer reduces exposure: review, no Irish-source automatic 50 mg dose.

common_clinician_facts.menopause: Confirmed postmenopausal endocrine state. Uncertain menopause or age <55 after hysterectomy requires hormone confirmation (FSH/LH/oestradiol). Amenorrhoea after chemotherapy is insufficient proof; return of ovarian function needs review. OFS combinations require a separately prescribed regimen.
common_clinician_facts.monitoring: NCCP baseline FBC, renal and liver profile and biochemical menopause checks when indicated. Bone density and lipids are risk/clinically directed, without an invented chemotherapy-cycle cadence, ANC/platelet ladder or routine ECG/echo. Exemestane additionally consider baseline 25-OH-vitamin D per SmPC.
common_clinician_facts.bone_guidance: NICE baseline adjuvant AI DXA except already on adjuvant bisphosphonates; 2025 joint guidance risk-based BMD reassessment 1–2 yearly for lower-risk patients, around 2 yearly on bone-protective treatment. These are guidance-based intervals, not NCCP routine cycle tests or AI hold thresholds.
common_clinician_facts.support: No routine steroid/antiemetic/G-CSF for these monotherapies. NCCP advises daily calcium/vitamin D supplementation and weight-bearing exercise; select the supplement product and dose with attention to diet, deficiency, organ function and existing supplements, without inventing a universal dose. Review adherence, joints, vasomotor symptoms, sexual/vaginal symptoms and interactions early.
common_clinician_facts.cross_suite: Patient guide, knowledge, consent, support, passport and timeline should share setting-specific duration, independent OFS boundary, symptom escalation and source-aware monitoring. Keep clinical trial numbers in clinician evidence only.

00254.purpose: After early breast cancer treatment, endocrine therapy reduces the risk of recurrence. In advanced disease, the aim is to control cancer and symptoms. Your setting determines the duration and follow-up.
00254.indication_text: Postmenopausal hormone-sensitive breast cancer in the NCCP adjuvant, switch-after-tamoxifen or advanced settings. The exact receptor and prior-treatment criteria remain a prescribing decision.
00254.administration_text: Swallow the tablet whole with water, with or without food. Do not replace a missed or vomited dose; resume the next scheduled dose.
00254.monitoring_summary: FBC, renal and liver profile. Confirm menopause; hormone tests may be needed if it is uncertain. Assess fracture risk and baseline bone density, particularly for adjuvant AI treatment. The NICE adjuvant baseline-DXA recommendation has an exception for patients already receiving adjuvant bisphosphonates. Assess symptoms, adherence and bone health at reviews. Repeat lipids and other blood tests when clinically indicated. Bone-density timing follows baseline results and fracture risk.

agents.explanation: Anastrozole blocks aromatase, an enzyme that makes oestrogen in fat and other tissues after menopause. Less oestrogen is available to stimulate hormone-sensitive breast cancer cells. This also explains effects such as hot flushes, vaginal dryness and bone thinning. It does not reliably switch off functioning ovaries; any ovarian-suppression treatment needs a separate prescription and checks.

sections.title: A continuous daily medicine
sections.text: Choose a consistent daily routine. There is no chemotherapy-style rest week or automatic restart date.

sections.title: Support joint symptoms
sections.text: Discuss safe physical activity, strength work and symptom treatment. Report symptoms early so the team can consider support or a planned switch instead of you stopping without advice.

sections.title: Keep the bone-health plan
sections.text: Ask when the baseline DXA result will be reviewed and when the next assessment is due. Calcium, vitamin D and bone medicines depend on diet, deficiency and fracture risk.

sections.title: If periods return
sections.text: Tell the oncology team about bleeding or return of periods, particularly after chemotherapy or if menopause was uncertain. Do not assume ovarian suppression is part of this monotherapy card.

questions.q: Do I have a treatment-free week?
questions.a: Take anastrozole once daily continuously. There is no planned week off. The treatment setting determines the intended duration.

questions.q: When are bloods, ECGs or echoes needed?
questions.a: FBC, renal and liver profile. Confirm menopause; hormone tests may be needed if it is uncertain. Assess fracture risk and baseline bone density, particularly for adjuvant AI treatment. The NICE adjuvant baseline-DXA recommendation has an exception for patients already receiving adjuvant bisphosphonates. Assess symptoms, adherence and bone health at reviews. Repeat lipids and other blood tests when clinically indicated. Bone-density timing follows baseline results and fracture risk. There is no routine ECG or echo schedule for anastrozole alone. Review cardiovascular risk factors and investigate cardiac symptoms when indicated.

questions.q: Which scans apply to me?
questions.a: After curative treatment, annual mammography is generally used for remaining breast tissue: both breasts after conservation or the opposite breast after unilateral mastectomy. The mastectomy side is not routinely mammographed. Routine CT, bone scans and tumour markers are not recommended for asymptomatic early-breast surveillance. New symptoms need assessment between appointments. For advanced breast cancer, response assessment is generally every two to four months, adapted to disease pace, sites, symptoms and treatment. Indolent disease may be reviewed less often; new symptoms can prompt earlier scans. The team chooses the imaging method; this is not a universal three-month CT chest/abdomen/pelvis order.

questions.q: What is my bone-health plan?
questions.a: Offer baseline DXA when starting an adjuvant aromatase inhibitor if not already receiving adjuvant bisphosphonates; assess fracture risk and relevant previous results. Under the 2025 joint guidance, patients with a T-score above −2.0 and no additional risk factors generally have risk and bone density reassessed every one to two years. Patients on bone-protective treatment generally have BMD reassessed about every two years. Fracture, substantial bone loss or a change in risk can require earlier review. The clinician selects the interval and any bone treatment; these are not automatic yearly scans for everyone.

questions.q: How long will treatment continue?
questions.a: After early breast cancer treatment, the team sets the intended total endocrine treatment length, taking account of any earlier tamoxifen. A course of several years may later be reviewed for extension according to recurrence risk, tolerance and bone health. Advanced-disease treatment is reviewed according to benefit and tolerance. A review date is not an automatic stop date.

questions.q: Do I need a port or home pump?
questions.a: No port or home infusion pump is needed for this medicine itself. Any separately prescribed medicine has its own access requirements.

questions.q: Can I use HRT, vaginal oestrogen or supplements?
questions.a: Check with the oncology team before starting any hormone-containing treatment, including vaginal oestrogen, or any new medicine or supplement. Some can oppose this treatment or change how it works. The team can suggest symptom treatments and decide whether specialist review is needed.

questions.q: What if periods return or menopause is uncertain?
questions.a: Tell the team promptly about a return of periods or new vaginal bleeding. No periods after chemotherapy does not always mean the ovaries have permanently stopped working. Hormone blood tests may be needed. Ovarian suppression, if prescribed, has its own schedule and monitoring.

questions.q: What should I do if symptoms make tablets difficult to continue?
questions.a: Tell the team early about joint pain, hot flushes, sleep, vaginal or sexual symptoms, fatigue or missed tablets. Support, a supervised break or a change of medicine may be possible. Agree the plan with the prescriber rather than changing or stopping treatment yourself.

questions.q: Do I need calcium and vitamin D?
questions.a: The NCCP regimen advises daily calcium and vitamin D supplementation. Ask the team or pharmacist to confirm the suitable product and dose, taking account of your diet, blood results, kidney health and any supplements you already take. Bone-protective medicines and bone-density checks follow your individual fracture-risk plan.

notes: Swallow the tablet whole, preferably after a meal; do not chew or crush it. Skip a missed dose and continue at the next scheduled time; do not double the dose.
Count earlier endocrine treatment when reviewing an adjuvant switch. Extended treatment is a separate decision.

evidence.title: Why this endocrine treatment is offered
evidence.population: Evidence depends on the treatment setting and previous endocrine medicines.
evidence.interpretation: For hormone-sensitive early breast cancer, endocrine treatment helps reduce the chance of the cancer returning. For advanced disease, it can help control cancer and symptoms.
evidence.limitations: Your likely benefit depends on your cancer, previous treatment and health. The treating team explains why this option fits your plan.
